## The 2016 Kaikōura Earthquake

At 12.02am on Monday 14 November 2016, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck central New Zealand, making it one of the most powerful — and complex — seismic events in the country's recorded history. [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

### A Remarkably Complex Rupture

What made this earthquake so scientifically extraordinary was its behaviour. At least 21 faults ruptured across 160 kilometres, with seismic energy leaping between them in ways that defied existing scientific models. [[3]](cite://3/1) Scientists had previously believed a fault could only trigger a neighbouring fault if they were less than about six kilometres apart — but the Kaikōura earthquake jumped across faults 15–20 kilometres apart. [[3]](cite://3/2) It is now considered one of the most complex earthquakes ever recorded. [[4]](cite://4/1)

One eyewitness, Scott Waterford, was literally astride the Kekerengu Fault as it ruptured. He described "the incredible noise" and watching trees lean over then right themselves, before the ground split open beneath his feet — his right leg going up and his left going down. The fault picked his house off its foundations and shunted it 10 metres away. [[4]](cite://4/2)

### Damage and Casualties

Two people lost their lives: one at Mt Lyford as a result of a heart attack, and another when a house collapsed in Kaikōura. [[2]](cite://2/2) Landslides cut off road and rail links to Kaikōura, stranding large numbers of visitors in the popular tourist town. [[2]](cite://2/3) State Highway 1 at Waipapa Bay was so badly mangled that the fault forced one section of road nearly four metres upward, while landslides blocked the road entirely around the headland — cutting locals off from schools and jobs. Repairing road and rail links was expected to take months, even years, and cost billions of dollars. [[5]](cite://5/1)

Beneath the sea, the earthquake unleashed a massive underwater landslide in the Kaikōura Canyon — a 1,200-metre-deep chasm south of the Kaikōura Peninsula. Around 50–60 metres of sediment roared down the canyon, scouring the sea floor to a depth of 20–30 metres and flowing at least 700 kilometres up the Hikurangi Trough. [[6]](cite://6/1)

### Tsunami

The earthquake also triggered the most significant local-source tsunami since 1947. [[3]](cite://3/3) Hundreds of people were evacuated from their homes to higher ground in Kaikōura and from low-lying suburbs of cities including Wellington and Christchurch. [[7]](cite://7/1) The maximum wave height onshore was 6–7 metres at Goose Bay, with 2.5-metre waves at Kaikōura and 1.6-metre waves reaching Wellington. [[8]](cite://8/1)[[9]](cite://9/1) At Little Pigeon Bay on Banks Peninsula, a three-metre wave shoved a holiday house off its foundations. [[8]](cite://8/2)

However, the tsunami's effects were dampened by a combination of low tide and coastal uplift along long stretches of the shoreline. [[8]](cite://8/3) There was also considerable confusion in the emergency response — in some areas, including Wellington, warning sirens weren't sounded until after the waves had already arrived. [[7]](cite://7/2)

## The 2016 Wellington Earthquake

The search results treat these as related but distinct events. The 2016 earthquake that affected Wellington was, in fact, the Kaikōura earthquake itself — but Wellington experienced it in a particularly significant way due to the unusual nature of the rupture.

Because the earthquake moved along at least five separate faults extending around 150 kilometres up the east coast of the South Island, its extraordinary release of energy was directed much closer to Wellington than to Kaikōura itself. [[10]](cite://10/1)

![embed-2](embed://2)

The earthquake necessitated the demolition of several modern office buildings erected on reclaimed land on Wellington's waterfront — a sobering outcome given that these were relatively new structures. [[11]](cite://11/1) The event reinforced long-standing warnings that Wellington faces significant seismic risk, with further large earthquakes considered not just likely but potentially overdue, meaning new buildings must be designed to survive such events and older buildings must be either strengthened or demolished. [[11]](cite://11/2)

The Kaikōura earthquake also challenged Wellington's tsunami preparedness. Warning sirens in some areas of the city weren't sounded until after the waves had arrived, exposing gaps in the city's civil defence response. [[7]](cite://7/3)

Would you like to explore more about what the Kaikōura earthquake revealed about Wellington's vulnerability to future seismic events?

2.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of Canterbury, New Zealand's South Island region, covering geography, history, culture, economy, and governance. Geographically, Canterbury features vast plains, the Southern Alps, braided rivers, and Christchurch, the "garden city." The region's geology was shaped by volcanic activity (Banks Peninsula 15-12 million years ago) and glaciation, with significant seismic activity including devastating earthquakes in 2010-2011 (6.3 magnitude, 185 deaths) and 2016 (7.8 magnitude Kaikōura). Historically, Ngāi Tahu Māori settled the region 600-700 years ago, establishing centers like Kaiapoi. European settlement began with Captain Cook (1770) and intensified after the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), with the Canterbury Association organizing settlement from 1850. The region developed strong agricultural heritage, transitioning from large estates to family farms, with sheep farming dominant (3.15 million head by 1885, 11% of national flock in 2012), supplemented by wheat production (62.5% of national) and expanding dairy operations (115% increase 2002-2012). Major irrigation schemes, including the Rangitātā diversion race (1945) and Central Plains Water scheme (2015), enabled intensive farming. Industrial development centered on farm-related processing and manufacturing, maintaining 11% of national manufacturing employment by 2013. Tourism accounted for 8.4% of jobs in 2010 but was severely impacted by the 2011 earthquake, with recovery underway by 2014. Transport infrastructure evolved significantly with the Lyttelton rail tunnel (1867), road tunnel (1964), Ōtira tunnel (1923), and Christchurch airport (opened 1940, first international airport 1950). Culturally, Canterbury developed a rich artistic heritage with notable figures including Samuel Butler, Denis Glover, Allen Curnow, and Rita Angus. The region has a strong sporting tradition, including rugby (Crusaders), tennis (Anthony Wilding), and hosted the 1974 Commonwealth Games. Governance evolved from provincial abolition (1876) through the Canterbury Regional Council (1989) to the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority (CERA) post-2011. In 2013, Canterbury had 478,623 residents (11.3% of New Zealand's population), predominantly European (86.2%), with recovery efforts including the Christchurch Central Recovery Plan (July 2012) and ongoing reconstruction.

3.document_title: Tsunamis in New Zealand: Hazards, History, and Warning Systems
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines tsunamis as a significant natural hazard in New Zealand. It covers tsunami generation through sea floor movements from earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and landslides, and explains how these waves travel at high speeds in deep ocean before slowing and increasing in height near shallow water. New Zealand's vulnerability stems from its extensive coastline and location in the Pacific Ocean, where approximately 80% of global tsunamis occur. The document provides historical analysis of major tsunami events including the 1855 Wairarapa earthquake tsunami (magnitude 8.1-8.2), the 1868 Peru-Chile tsunami (magnitude 9.0) that devastated the Chatham Islands and Banks Peninsula, the 1947 Gisborne tsunamis, and the 1960 Chile tsunami (magnitude 9.5). Archaeological evidence indicates Māori settlements shifted from coastal to inland sites in the mid-15th century due to tsunami inundation. The document details tsunami hazards including local earthquakes on submarine faults, the Hikurangi Trough subduction zone, landslides, and offshore volcanoes. Approximately a dozen tsunamis exceeding one meter strike New Zealand annually. New Zealand's dual warning system includes the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center for distant tsunamis (providing 12+ hours warning) and natural warning signs for local tsunamis (arriving within minutes). Key safety measures include tsunami gauge networks, evacuation zone maps, and public alert systems. The principle "If LONG or STRONG, GET GONE!" is emphasized for earthquake-triggered tsunamis. Only one official death from tsunamis has been recorded since European settlement.

21.document_title: The 2016 Kaikōura Earthquake: Comprehensive Scientific Research, Fault Rupture Analysis, and Community Impact
21.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the 2016 Kaikōura Earthquake (magnitude 7.8), one of New Zealand's most significant natural events. The earthquake ruptured at least nine interconnected faults across 120 kilometres of the Kaikōura coast, with displacements up to 12 metres on the Kekerengu Fault. Scientists including Russ Van Dissen and Tim Little investigated how seismic energy jumps between faults. The rupture extended from Culverden to Cook Strait, triggering over 8,000 aftershocks and unexpected surface breaks on previously thought-inactive faults like Papatea and Leader. The earthquake lifted 80 kilometres of coastline, with dramatic coastal uplift at Waipapa Bay where the Papatea Fault forced a 700-metre stretch of coastline 5.5 metres out of the sea. The event triggered approximately 100,000 landslides and caused significant landscape transformation. Marine geologists aboard the research vessel Tangaroa documented unprecedented underwater effects, including a 1.4-metre vertical slip on the Needles Fault. Using advanced drone technology and 3D mapping, researchers document fault interactions to improve New Zealand's National Seismic Hazard Model and enhance building codes. The research reveals complex plate tectonics shaped by the collision of the Australian and Pacific Plates, with the Marlborough fault system accommodating plate-boundary movement at three centimetres per year through periodic violent earthquakes.

26.document_title: The End of the Everywhere Bird: Red-Billed Gulls in Decline
26.document_summary: This article examines the dramatic decline of red-billed gulls (tarāpunga) in New Zealand, particularly at the Kaikōura colony, which has plummeted from 15,000-20,000 birds in the 1980s-90s to approximately 3,800 by December 2023. Researcher Jim Mills spent 55 years (1964-2017) monitoring and banding over 76,000 chicks, creating one of the world's largest avian databases. Red-billed gulls face multiple interconnected threats including predation by feral cats, disease, avian influenza, and critically, starvation due to changing ocean conditions. The gulls depend on krill upwellings off the Kaikōura coast, which require specific water temperature patterns; warm water intrusions prevent krill from reaching the surface. Birds have become smaller and lighter over decades—signs of chronic starvation—with only about half of breeding females attempting nesting. Wildlife rehabilitator Sabrina Luecht documents starving gulls at Project WellBird, warning of potential extinction within two to three decades. Mills' research contributed to the global "One-Third for the Birds" study, revealing that seabird breeding success declines when forage fish fall below one-third of historical maximums. While Otago's gull populations are increasing due to abundant krill, conservation efforts in Kaikōura include citizen science projects and predator control. The article emphasizes how these overlooked birds possess complex social structures and remarkable adaptability, yet remain vulnerable to environmental changes and human indifference.

[Page 1] By Kate Evans Last year’s earthquake is now believed to be one of the most complex ever recorded. On November 14, two minutes after midnight, Scott Waterford had just gone to bed when the Kaikōura earthquake shook him out of it. Still in his undies, Waterford took shelter in a doorway. Then, as the shuddering intensified, he jumped off the veranda and ran into the paddock. “All I remember is the incredible noise, and because of the full moon I could see everything twisting and bending.” He saw trees lean over then stand back up, and power lines spark as they were ripped from his house. A minute or so after the shaking started, the ground split open. “I was standing there watching my house and trying not to fall over, and suddenly my right leg went up and my left leg went down. I was still swearing quite a lot.” Waterford was literally astride the Kekerengu Fault as it tore towards the sea. That’s when he started running. He sprinted across the paddocks to his boss’s house, leaping over a few fences on the way. Later, he discovered the fault had picked his house up off its foundations and shunted it 10 metres away. Scientists knew about this ‘lightning and thunder’ effect in theory, but only a couple of people have experienced it in person: first the shaking, then the land breaking. “The shaking moves faster than the fault unzips,” says Russ van Dissen, a GNS Science earthquake geologist who is an expert on the Kekerengu Fault. “Through instruments we know that this happens, that they travel at different speeds—but to have a person right at that place and see it with their own eyes is amazing.”

The earthquake affected approximately 52,000 square kilometers, causing extensive infrastructure damage yet resulting in only 10 fatalities. The event significantly impacted Wellington's development and construction practices, with evidence suggesting a pattern of major seismic activity along the fault over 10,000 years.

3.fileDescription: The November 14 Kaikōura earthquake in New Zealand revealed unprecedented scientific discoveries about seismic activity. The event, now considered one of the most complex earthquakes ever recorded, ruptured at least 21 faults across 160 kilometres. By Kate Evans
Last year’s earthquake is now believed to be one of the most complex ever recorded.
On November 14, two minutes after midnight, Scott Waterford had just gone to bed when the Kaikōura earthquake shook him out of it.
Still in his undies, Waterford took shelter in a doorway. Then, as the shuddering intensified, he jumped off the veranda and ran into the paddock.
“All I remember is the incredible noise, and because of the full moon I could see everything twisting and bending.”
He saw trees lean over then stand back up, and power lines spark as they were ripped from his house.
A minute or so after the shaking started, the ground split open.
“I was standing there watching my house and trying not to fall over, and suddenly my right leg went up and my left leg went down. I was still swearing quite a lot.”
Waterford was literally astride the Kekerengu Fault as it tore towards the sea.

That’s when he started running. He sprinted across the paddocks to his boss’s house, leaping over a few fences on the way. Later, he discovered the fault had picked his house up off its foundations and shunted it 10 metres away.
Scientists knew about this ‘lightning and thunder’ effect in theory, but only a couple of people have experienced it in person: first the shaking,
then the land breaking.

“The shaking moves faster than the fault unzips,” says Russ van Dissen, a GNS Science earthquake geologist who is an expert on the Kekerengu Fault. “Through instruments we know that this happens, that they travel at different speeds—but to have a person right at that place and see it with their own eyes is amazing.”

Despite ground shaking below design code thresholds (0.6-0.8g vs. required 1.0g), approximately 40 Wellington buildings suffered severe damage, including modern structures like Statistics House (2005) and the Asteron Centre (2010). The article identifies three critical factors: the earthquake's unusually long duration (90 seconds), frequency characteristics (1-2 seconds) that resonated with 8-15-storey buildings causing amplified swaying, and liquefaction effects on reclaimed land creating a "bowl-of-jelly" amplification. These combined factors created a "perfect quake" scenario that current building codes fail to anticipate. The author argues that New Zealand's building codes rely on minimum one-in-500-year standards and should instead adopt advanced seismic technologies like base isolation, damping systems, and damage-resistant design. The article calls for a fundamental rethink of building standards, viewing structures as intergenerational assets rather than short-term investments, and designing buildings to endure 100+ years against nature's unpredictable forces.

Thousands of rescuers pressed on in their search for survivors of a New Year's Day quake that killed at least 77 people in Japan, hoping to save as many as they can within a three day survival window which ends on Thursday afternoon (early this evening NZT). "There's little time left until it's 72 hours since the quake," Masuhiro Izumiya, the mayor of hard hit Suzu city, said on Wednesday evening at a regional disaster response meeting. "We really need to muster all of our remaining strength to continue rescue efforts." Survival rates drop off 72 hours after the quake, according to emergency responders. Severed roads and the remote location of the worst hit areas have complicated rescue efforts. Nearly 600 tremors have hit the Noto peninsula since the main quake, raising fears of landslides and further damage to infrastructure. "Compared to other disasters the road situation into Wajima is very bad. I feel it's taking longer than usual for assistance to arrive," Shunsaku Kohriki, a medical worker, told Reuters in Wajima city.
